grammar.title: Inversion after negative and limiting adverbials
grammar.explanation_pt:
Quando uma expressão **negativa ou restritiva** abre a frase, invertemos sujeito e auxiliar, **como numa pergunta**. O efeito é **formal e enfático**.

**Estrutura:** expressão + **auxiliar + sujeito** + verbo
(se não houver auxiliar, use **do / does / did**)

**1. Never / Rarely / Seldom / Hardly ever**
- "**Never before had** a product sold so fast."
- "**Rarely do** start-ups survive their first five years."

**2. Not only... but (also)**
- "**Not only did** they lose money, **but** they **also** lost their reputation."

**3. Little** (= não fazer ideia)
- "**Little did** they **know** that a small start-up would replace them."

**4. Sequências rápidas: No sooner... than / Hardly... when / Scarcely... when** (geralmente com past perfect)
- "**No sooner had** they launched the app **than** it crashed."
- "**Hardly had** the CEO resigned **when** the share price rose."

**5. Only + expressão de tempo/condição** → a inversão vem na **oração principal**:
- "**Only when** sales collapsed **did they realize** the problem."
- "**Only after** the merger **was** the extent of the debt revealed."
- "**Not until** 2010 **did** the company **launch** its first app."
- "**Only by** listening to customers **can** you succeed."

**6. Expressões com "no"**
- "**Under no circumstances should** you share your password."
- "**On no account must** this information leave the room."
- "**At no time did** the board **consider** selling."
- "**In no way is** this a criticism."

⚠️ **Não inverta** se a expressão não for negativa/restritiva ou não estiver no início: "They **had never** seen..." (sem inversão).
⚠️ **Not only** no meio da frase não inverte: "They **not only** lost money **but also**..."

Not only is it cheaper, but it's also faster.
No sooner had I arrived than the phone rang.
Hardly had we started when the power went off.

dialogue.title: Post-mortem
dialogue.context_pt: Dois ex-diretores de uma rede de locadoras de vídeo (empresa fictícia) relembram o fim do negócio numa entrevista para um podcast.

lines.en: So, looking back, when did you realize the company was in trouble?

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.en: Honestly? Far too late. Only when our biggest stores started closing did we accept that streaming wasn't a fad.
lines.pt: Sinceramente? Tarde demais. Só quando nossas maiores lojas começaram a fechar aceitamos que o streaming não era moda passageira.

lines.speaker: Paula
lines.en: And the frustrating thing is that we'd been warned. A young engineer presented a streaming prototype in 2006. Not only did we reject it, but we also cut her team's budget.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Why?
lines.pt: Por quê?

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.en: Complacency. We had 70% of the market. Never before had we faced a real competitor, so we assumed we never would.

lines.speaker: Paula

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: That's quite an ending. What's the lesson for leaders today?

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.en: Under no circumstances should you assume your success will last. Rarely does disruption come from where you expect it.

listening.title: The innovator's dilemma
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de administração explica a teoria da inovação disruptiva.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: In 1997, the Harvard professor Clayton Christensen published The Innovator's Dilemma, a book that changed how business leaders think about innovation. His central question was a puzzling one: why do successful, well-managed companies fail? His answer was that they often fail precisely because they do the right things — they listen to their best customers and focus on improving their most profitable products. Meanwhile, a new technology appears at the bottom of the market. At first, it's cheaper, simpler and, frankly, worse. Established firms ignore it, because their best customers don't want it. But the new technology improves, and by the time it's good enough for mainstream customers, it's too late. Not only have the newcomers taken the low end of the market; they've learned how to move up. Kodak is often cited as an example: one of its own engineers built an early digital camera in 1975, yet the company struggled to embrace the technology that eventually helped to bring it down.

questions.q: What was Christensen's central question?
questions.answer: Why do successful, well-managed companies fail?

questions.q: Why do established companies ignore the new technology?
questions.answer: Because their best customers don't want it at first.

questions.q: What is the new technology like at first?
questions.answer: Cheaper, simpler and worse.

questions.q: Why is Kodak cited as an example?
questions.answer: Its engineer built an early digital camera in 1975, but it struggled to embrace digital technology.

reading.title: Brazil's banking revolution
reading.text: For decades, opening a bank account in Brazil was, for many people, a frustrating experience. Fees were high, branches were crowded and the paperwork seemed endless. Large numbers of adults, particularly among lower-income groups, had no account at all. Then, in the 2010s, a wave of digital banks began to change the picture. Offering free accounts and credit cards that could be managed entirely through an app, companies such as Nubank attracted millions of customers who had long been ignored or poorly served by traditional institutions. Never before had so many Brazilians been able to open an account in a matter of minutes, from their phones. The traditional banks, at first, appeared unconcerned. Only when the new players had gathered tens of millions of customers did several of them respond seriously, launching their own digital brands and cutting fees. The changes did not stop there. In 2020, the Central Bank launched Pix, an instant payment system that is free for individuals. Not only did Pix make transfers immediate, but it also allowed small businesses and informal workers to accept payments without expensive card machines. Its adoption was remarkably fast: within a few years it had become one of the most widely used payment methods in the country. Seldom has a public innovation been embraced so quickly. Experts still debate the risks, from fraud to rising household debt. Yet few would deny that, in little more than a decade, the relationship between Brazilians and their money has been transformed.

questions.q: What problems did many Brazilians face with traditional banks?
questions.answer: High fees, crowded branches and endless paperwork; many had no account.

questions.q: What did digital banks offer?
questions.answer: Free accounts and credit cards managed entirely through an app.

questions.q: When did traditional banks respond seriously?
questions.answer: Only when the new players had gathered tens of millions of customers.

questions.q: What two benefits of Pix are mentioned?
questions.answer: Immediate transfers and allowing small businesses to accept payments without card machines.

writing.model:
The phone that swallowed the world

When Apple unveiled the first iPhone in January 2007, many industry experts were unimpressed. It had no physical keyboard, it was expensive, and at launch it couldn't run apps made by other companies. Little did they know that they were looking at the device that would transform not only the phone industry but almost every industry it touched.

At the time, the market leaders were Nokia and BlackBerry. Seldom had any company dominated a sector as completely as Nokia did in the mid-2000s, and BlackBerry was the undisputed favourite of business users. Both believed that their strengths — reliable hardware and physical keyboards — would protect them. Only when their customers began switching in large numbers did they accept that the rules of the game had changed.

What made the smartphone so disruptive? Not only did it combine a phone, a music player and an internet browser in one device, but, with the launch of the App Store in 2008, it became a platform on which other businesses could be built. No sooner had the store opened than developers began creating products that nobody had imagined: ride-hailing, mobile banking, food delivery, dating apps.

The consequences went far beyond technology. Cameras, maps, alarm clocks and even torches were absorbed into a single device. Rarely has a product rendered so many others obsolete so quickly.

There is, of course, a darker side. Not until years later did researchers and parents begin to seriously question the effects of constant connectivity on attention and mental health, a debate that continues today.

The lesson for business leaders is clear. Under no circumstances should a company assume that today's market leadership guarantees tomorrow's survival. In technology, as Nokia discovered, the fall can be as fast as the rise.

culture_note.title: "Disrupt" — de palavra negativa a elogio
culture_note.text_pt: Tradicionalmente, **disrupt** significa perturbar, interromper ("protesters disrupted the meeting"). Desde a teoria de Clayton Christensen, nos anos 1990, **disruptive** virou elogio no mundo dos negócios. Hoje, muitos críticos acham a palavra desgastada — usada para qualquer startup, mesmo sem inovação real.

summary_pt: Expressão negativa/restritiva no início + auxiliar + sujeito.

grammar.title: Nominalisation and formal register
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Nominalização** = transformar **verbos** ou **adjetivos** em **substantivos**. O resultado é um texto mais **denso, impessoal e objetivo** — o estilo de relatórios, artigos e textos acadêmicos.

**Comparação:**
- Fala: "Prices **went up** sharply, so people **bought** less."
- Formal: "The sharp **rise** in prices led to a **fall** in consumption."

**Sufixos comuns:**
- **-tion / -sion:** introduce → introduction, decide → decision, expand → expansion
- **-ment:** develop → development, improve → improvement
- **-ance / -ence:** perform → performance, depend → dependence
- **-ity:** flexible → flexibility, secure → security
- **-ness:** aware → awareness, effective → effectiveness
- **-al:** arrive → arrival, refuse → refusal
- Mesma forma: increase, decline, rise, fall, change, cut, demand

**Como nominalizar:**
1. Transforme o verbo principal em substantivo.
2. O sujeito vira **possessivo** ou **of**: "The government **regulated** apps" → "The government's **regulation** of apps" / "**the regulation of** apps **by** the government".
3. Advérbio vira **adjetivo**: "increased **sharply**" → "a **sharp** increase".
4. Conectores viram **verbos/preposições de causa**: because/so → **led to, resulted in, caused, due to, as a result of**.

**Collocations formais com substantivos:**
carry out (research / an investigation / a survey) · make (an improvement / a recommendation / a contribution) · have (an impact / an effect on) · take (measures / steps / action) · reach (a conclusion / an agreement) · pose (a threat / a risk)

⚠️ **Cuidado com o exagero:** nominalização demais deixa o texto pesado e difícil. Equilibre com verbos fortes.

listening.title: The four-day week
listening.context_pt: Uma jornalista apresenta resultados de testes da semana de quatro dias.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: One of the most talked-about experiments in the world of work in recent years has been the four-day week. In 2022, a large pilot programme in the UK involved around sixty companies, whose employees moved to a four-day week with no loss of pay, on the condition that productivity was maintained. The results, published in 2023, attracted international attention. Most of the participating companies said they would continue with the new schedule. Researchers reported reductions in stress and burnout among employees, as well as improvements in sleep and work-life balance. Similar trials have since been carried out in other countries, including Brazil. Critics point out, however, that the companies involved chose to take part, which may have influenced the results, and that the model is far harder to implement in sectors such as healthcare or retail. The debate, in other words, is far from over.

questions.q: What was the condition of the UK pilot?
questions.answer: No loss of pay, as long as productivity was maintained.

questions.q: What did most participating companies decide?
questions.answer: To continue with the four-day week.

questions.q: What improvements did researchers report?
questions.answer: Less stress and burnout, better sleep and work-life balance.

questions.q: What criticisms are mentioned?
questions.answer: Companies chose to take part, and it is harder in sectors like healthcare or retail.

reading.title: Working for the algorithm
reading.text: The expansion of app-based work has been one of the most significant changes in the labour market of the past decade. In Brazil, as in many other countries, the growth of ride-hailing and food delivery platforms has created opportunities for hundreds of thousands of people, particularly during periods of high unemployment. For many workers, the attraction lies in the flexibility these platforms offer: the ability to choose when and how long to work, and the absence of a boss in the traditional sense. However, this flexibility comes at a price. Unlike conventional employees, most platform workers do not have access to paid holidays, sick pay or guaranteed minimum earnings. Their income depends on fluctuations in demand and on decisions made by algorithms over which they have little control or understanding. The suspension of an account, for example, can mean the immediate loss of a worker's livelihood, often without a clear explanation. These concerns have led to growing pressure for regulation. Governments in several countries, including Brazil, have attempted to introduce rules guaranteeing minimum standards of pay and social protection, though such proposals have frequently met with resistance from both companies and some workers, who fear the loss of flexibility. The challenge for policymakers, therefore, lies in the development of a model that combines the advantages of flexibility with an adequate level of security. The outcome of this debate will have a profound impact not only on platform workers, but on the future of work as a whole.

questions.q: What attracts many workers to platforms?
questions.answer: Flexibility: choosing when and how long to work, and no traditional boss.

questions.q: What do most platform workers lack?
questions.answer: Paid holidays, sick pay and guaranteed minimum earnings.

questions.q: Why can an account suspension be serious?
questions.answer: It can mean the immediate loss of a livelihood, often without explanation.

questions.q: Why have some workers resisted regulation?
questions.answer: They fear losing flexibility.

writing.model:
Report on the hybrid working trial

Introduction
The aim of this report is to evaluate the results of the six-month hybrid working trial carried out in the marketing and finance departments between January and June, and to make recommendations regarding its continuation. The findings are based on an online survey of 85 employees, interviews with team leaders and an analysis of performance data.

Findings
Overall, the introduction of hybrid working was well received. Approximately 80% of respondents reported an improvement in their work-life balance, largely as a result of the reduction in commuting time. Performance data showed no decline in productivity; in fact, the finance department recorded a slight increase in the number of tasks completed on time.

However, the trial also revealed some concerns. Several employees mentioned a lack of contact with colleagues and a sense of isolation, particularly among new staff. Team leaders also highlighted difficulties in the coordination of projects when team members were rarely in the office on the same days. In addition, the absence of clear guidelines led to some confusion regarding availability and response times.

Recommendations
In light of these findings, the following measures are recommended:
• the continuation of the hybrid model, with a minimum of two office days per week;
• the introduction of fixed "team days" to facilitate collaboration;
• the creation of a mentoring programme for new employees;
• the publication of clear guidelines on working hours and communication.

Conclusion
The trial has demonstrated that hybrid working can lead to greater employee satisfaction without any loss of productivity. Provided that the issues of isolation and coordination are addressed, the adoption of the model on a permanent basis would be of considerable benefit to the company.

grammar.title: Advanced modals: probability and attitude
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Graduando a probabilidade (do mais certo ao menos certo):**
- **will / be bound to / be sure to / be certain to** → certeza: "There**'s bound to** be resistance." (com certeza)
- **should / ought to** → expectativa lógica: "The report **should be** ready by Friday." (é o esperado)
- **may well / might well / could well** → **bem provável** (o "well" aumenta a chance): "She **might well** get the job."
- **may / might / could** → possível
- **might just / could just** → pequena chance (às vezes com esperança): "It **might just** work!"
- **be unlikely to / I doubt** → improvável

**2. May / might as well** → "é melhor / tanto faz, então..." (sugestão sem entusiasmo, porque não há opção melhor):
- "The meeting is cancelled. We **may as well** go home."
- "Nobody's listening. I **might as well** be talking to a wall." (= é como se...)

**3. Could hardly / can't possibly** → quase impossível:
- "I **could hardly** say no to my boss." / "We **can't possibly** finish by Monday."

**4. Would para expectativa e crítica:**
- "You**'d think** a manager **would** know that." (seria de esperar)
- "She **would** say that, wouldn't she?" (típico dela)
- "I**'d have thought** so." (eu acharia que sim)

**5. No passado:** might well have, is bound to have, should have (expectativa: "They **should have arrived** by now.")

rows: be bound to / be sure to

listening.title: What makes a team work?
listening.context_pt: Um consultor fala sobre pesquisas sobre equipes eficazes.

lines.speaker: Consultant
lines.en: A few years ago, Google ran an internal research project, known as Project Aristotle, to find out why some of its teams performed better than others. You'd think the answer would be about talent — put the smartest people together and you're bound to succeed. But that's not what they found. According to the company's own summary, the most important factor was psychological safety: whether team members feel safe to take risks, ask questions and admit mistakes without being embarrassed or punished. The concept was developed by Amy Edmondson, a professor at Harvard Business School. Her early research in hospitals produced a surprising result: the better teams appeared to report more errors — not because they made more, she concluded, but because people felt safe enough to talk about them. So, if you're a leader, the message is clear. Your team may well be hiding problems from you. And if they are, you might as well be flying blind.

reading.title: The humble leader
reading.text: For much of the twentieth century, the ideal leader was imagined as a confident, decisive figure who had all the answers. That image may well be changing. A growing body of research suggests that some of the most effective leaders combine ambition with a quality that is rarely associated with power: humility. In his influential study of companies that had made the leap from good to great performance, the management writer Jim Collins described what he called "Level 5 leaders" — executives who blended intense professional will with personal modesty. They were quick to give credit to others for success and to take responsibility for failure. Later studies have pointed in a similar direction, linking humble leadership with greater team engagement and learning. Why should humility matter so much? One explanation is that no leader, however talented, can possibly know everything in a complex organization. Leaders who admit what they don't know are more likely to ask for input, and their teams are more likely to offer it. Arrogant leaders, by contrast, are bound to hear only what they want to hear. None of this means that leaders should be passive or indecisive. Teams still need direction, and there will be moments when someone simply has to decide. But the old idea that admitting a mistake is a sign of weakness looks increasingly outdated. You'd think, after decades of evidence, that this lesson would be widely accepted. In many workplaces, however, it is still waiting to be learned.

Subject: Hello from your new team leader

Dear all,

As most of you will know by now, I'm joining the customer experience team as your new leader from Monday. I wanted to take this opportunity to introduce myself and share a few thoughts about how I like to work.

I've spent the last eight years in customer service, first as an agent and later as a supervisor, so I have a pretty good idea of what your days look like — the good, the bad and the frustrating. That said, every team is different, and I'm bound to have a lot to learn about how things work here. Over the next few weeks, I'd like to meet each of you individually. The meetings should take about thirty minutes, and Ana will send out a schedule shortly.

In terms of style, I try to be hands-on without micromanaging. I'll set clear goals, but I trust you to decide how to reach them. I'd much rather you came to me with a problem early than tried to hide it — mistakes are inevitable, and you'll find I'm the first to own mine.

You may well have heard that the company is planning to introduce a new support platform later this year. I know changes like this can cause anxiety, and there may well be some difficult moments during the transition. However, I can promise that you'll be involved in the process from the start. After all, you know our customers better than anyone, so it would hardly make sense to plan this without you.

Finally, my door — or my Teams chat — is always open. If you have questions, ideas or concerns, you might as well send them now rather than wait for our meeting!

Looking forward to working with you all.

Best wishes,
Gabriela

grammar.title: Rhetorical devices and cleft sentences
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Regra de três (tricolon)** — três elementos paralelos soam completos e memoráveis:
- "Our app is **faster, cheaper and safer**."
- "**We listened, we learned, and we built** something better."

**2. Perguntas retóricas** — envolvem o público (você responde logo em seguida):
- "**How many of you** have waited an hour for a doctor's appointment? **Exactly.**"
- "**So, why does this matter?** Because..."

**3. Contraste e antítese:**
- "It's **not about** working harder; **it's about** working smarter."
- "**Yesterday**, it took three days. **Today**, it takes three minutes."

**4. Repetição (anáfora)** — repetir o início das frases:
- "**Every day**, families lose time. **Every day**, businesses lose money. **Every day**, we wait."

**5. Cleft sentences para foco** (revisão e expansão do B2):
- **What** + oração + **is/was**: "**What we need is** a simpler solution." / "**What surprised us was** the demand."
- **All** + oração (= a única coisa): "**All you need is** a phone."
- **The reason (why)... is that**: "**The reason why** we're different **is that** we listen."
- **The thing / The problem / The truth is (that)**: "**The problem is that** nobody trusts the current system."
- **It is/was... that/who**: "**It was** our customers **who** gave us this idea."

**6. Signposting** — sinaliza a estrutura:
- Começo: "I'd like to start by... / Let me begin with a question."
- Transição: "Let's move on to... / This brings me to... / Turning now to..."
- Ênfase: "I'd like to stress that... / The key point here is..."
- Fim: "To wrap up... / Let me leave you with one thought..."

lines.pt: "Olá, meu nome é Malu e sou fundadora da FeiraJá. Nosso app conecta pequenos agricultores a restaurantes..."

lines.speaker: Mentor
lines.en: Stop there. You've lost them already. Don't start with your name — start with the problem. Hook them.
lines.pt: Para aí. Você já perdeu eles. Não comece com seu nome — comece com o problema. Prenda a atenção.

lines.speaker: Malu
lines.en: Right. "How much of the food grown in Brazil never reaches a plate? According to some estimates, a significant share is wasted along the way. What small farmers need isn't charity — it's a direct route to buyers."
lines.pt: Certo. "Quanto da comida produzida no Brasil nunca chega a um prato? Segundo algumas estimativas, uma parcela significativa é desperdiçada pelo caminho. Do que os pequenos agricultores precisam não é caridade — é um caminho direto até os compradores."

lines.speaker: Mentor
lines.en: Much better. Now the solution, and keep it simple.
lines.pt: Muito melhor. Agora a solução, e mantenha simples.

lines.speaker: Malu
lines.en: "FeiraJá connects farmers directly with restaurants. Fresher food, fairer prices and less waste. Restaurants order by 8 p.m.; the food arrives the next morning."
lines.pt: "A FeiraJá conecta agricultores diretamente a restaurantes. Comida mais fresca, preços mais justos e menos desperdício. Os restaurantes pedem até as 20h; a comida chega na manhã seguinte."

lines.speaker: Mentor
lines.en: Great use of the rule of three. What about traction? Investors will want numbers.
lines.pt: Ótimo uso da regra de três. E a tração? Investidores vão querer números.

lines.speaker: Malu
lines.en: "This brings me to our results. In twelve months, we've grown from five farmers to two hundred. It was our first restaurant clients who asked us to expand — and that's why we're here today."
lines.pt: "Isso me leva aos nossos resultados. Em doze meses, passamos de cinco para duzentos agricultores. Foram nossos primeiros restaurantes clientes que pediram para expandirmos — e é por isso que estamos aqui hoje."

lines.speaker: Mentor
lines.en: Excellent. Finish with a clear call to action, and you've got it.
lines.pt: Excelente. Termine com uma chamada para ação clara e está pronto.

listening.title: Three tricks from the ancient world
listening.context_pt: Um professor de oratória explica recursos retóricos clássicos.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: More than two thousand years ago, Aristotle argued that persuasion rests on three pillars: ethos, your credibility; pathos, the emotions you create; and logos, your logic and evidence. Notice, by the way, that even his theory comes in three parts. The rule of three is everywhere in rhetoric. Julius Caesar's famous message, often quoted as "veni, vidi, vici" — "I came, I saw, I conquered" — is perhaps the most famous example. Why does it work? Psychologists suggest that three is the smallest number that creates a pattern. Two items feel like a comparison; four start to feel like a list. Three feels complete. The second trick is antithesis — putting opposites side by side. Think of Neil Armstrong's line about "one small step for man" and "one giant leap for mankind". And the third is the rhetorical question, which turns a lecture into a conversation. So, what do these techniques have in common? They make your message easier to remember. And in a pitch, what matters most is what people remember after you've left the room.

questions.q: What are Aristotle's three pillars of persuasion?
questions.answer: Ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion) and logos (logic and evidence).

questions.q: Why does the rule of three work?
questions.answer: Three is the smallest number that creates a pattern; it feels complete.

questions.q: What is antithesis?
questions.answer: Putting opposites side by side.

questions.q: What do the three techniques have in common?
questions.answer: They make the message easier to remember.

reading.title: Why most pitches fail
reading.text: Every year, thousands of founders stand in front of investors hoping to secure funding. Most of them fail — and, according to experienced investors, the reason is rarely the idea itself. What sinks most pitches is the way the idea is communicated. The first mistake is starting in the wrong place. Many founders open with their company history or a detailed description of their technology. Investors, however, want to understand the problem before they care about the solution. A strong pitch begins with a pain point the audience can feel — ideally one that is large, urgent and growing. The second mistake is trying to say too much. Faced with a short time slot, nervous presenters often try to cram every feature onto their slides. The result is confusion. What investors remember is a single clear message: who the product is for, what it does, and why it is better than the alternatives. The third mistake is neglecting evidence. Enthusiasm is necessary, but it is not sufficient. Investors want to see traction — paying customers, growth rates, partnerships — that proves the idea works outside the founder's imagination. Finally, many pitches simply end. The speaker reaches the last slide, says "thank you" and waits for questions. A compelling pitch, by contrast, finishes with a clear call to action: what the founder is asking for and what the investor will gain. The best founders understand that a pitch is not a lecture. It is the beginning of a relationship. And, as with any relationship, first impressions matter enormously.

questions.q: What sinks most pitches, according to investors?
questions.answer: The way the idea is communicated, not the idea itself.

questions.q: Where should a strong pitch begin?
questions.answer: With a pain point the audience can feel.

questions.q: What is traction? Give examples.
questions.answer: Evidence the idea works: paying customers, growth rates, partnerships.

questions.q: How should a compelling pitch end?
questions.answer: With a clear call to action: what is asked and what the investor gains.

writing.model:
Pitch script: AulaViva

How many of you had a teacher who changed your life? (Pause.) Now imagine if that teacher, after retiring, could keep changing lives — from home, a few hours a week.

That's the idea behind AulaViva.

Let me start with the problem. Across Brazil, many students who struggle at school have no access to extra help. Private tutoring is expensive, and public schools are often overloaded. At the same time, thousands of experienced teachers retire every year. They have the knowledge, the patience and, very often, the desire to keep teaching. What's missing is a bridge between these two groups.

AulaViva is that bridge. We're an online platform that connects retired teachers with students who need support. Sessions are affordable for families, flexible for teachers and free for students from low-income households, thanks to sponsorship from local businesses.

This brings me to our results. We launched a pilot in two cities last year. In six months, 120 retired teachers joined the platform and delivered more than 3,000 hours of tutoring. Participating schools reported that most students improved their maths grades. But it was the teachers who surprised us most: many told us they felt useful and connected again.

So, what makes us different? It's not just a tutoring app; it's a community. The reason why our teachers stay is that they feel valued, not just paid.

Now, let's look at the opportunity. Brazil has millions of students who could benefit, and the number of retired teachers is growing every year. We're ready to expand to ten more cities.

To wrap up, we're looking for an investment of two million reais to fund this expansion and develop our mobile app. In return, we're offering a 15% stake in a company with proven impact, a scalable model and a mission that matters.

What we're asking for today isn't charity. It's a partnership. Thank you.

culture_note.title: Pitch à americana
culture_note.text_pt: O estilo de pitch do Vale do Silício é **direto, confiante e otimista** — às vezes até exagerado para padrões britânicos ou brasileiros. No Reino Unido, um tom mais **modesto** e algum humor autodepreciativo costumam funcionar melhor. Conheça seu público: o que soa "confiante" em São Francisco pode soar "arrogante" em Londres.

summary_pt: Regra de três, perguntas retóricas, antítese e repetição.

Signposting: Let me start by... / This brings me to... / To wrap up...
